lesson.title: The Falling Half of the Wave: Differentiating Cosine
lesson.summary: The same limit strategy used for sine, now applied to the angle addition formula for cosine, shows that the derivative of cosine is negative sine, with the sign explained by where cosine is increasing and decreasing.
lesson.body:
Having just found that the derivative of sin x is cos x, it is natural to ask what happens with cos x itself. The derivation follows exactly the same path as before, which is worth noticing: once you have the pattern for one trigonometric derivative, the machinery transfers directly to the next one, rather than requiring a completely new idea.

Start again from the limit definition: d/dx cos x = lim(h to 0) [cos(x+h) - cos x] / h. This time expand cos(x+h) using its own angle addition identity, cos(x+h) = cos x cos h - sin x sin h. Substituting, the numerator becomes cos x cos h - sin x sin h - cos x, which regroups as cos x (cos h - 1) - sin x sin h. Dividing by h and splitting the limit gives cos x * lim(h to 0) (cos h - 1)/h - sin x * lim(h to 0) (sin h)/h.

The same two limits from the sine derivation reappear here: (cos h - 1)/h approaches 0, and (sin h)/h approaches 1. Substituting these in gives cos x * 0 - sin x * 1 = -sin x. So d/dx cos x = -sin x. The minus sign is not an accident of algebra, it reflects something visible on the graph: wherever sin x is positive, meaning the cosine curve is on its way down from a peak toward a trough, the slope of cosine is indeed negative, and wherever sin x is negative, cosine is climbing back up with a positive slope.

A worked check at x = pi/3 confirms the formula without circular reasoning. Using the angle addition identity directly, cos(pi/3 + 0.001) = cos(pi/3)cos(0.001) - sin(pi/3)sin(0.001). With cos(pi/3) = 0.5, sin(pi/3) about 0.86603, cos(0.001) about 0.9999995, and sin(0.001) about 0.001, this works out to about 0.5(0.9999995) - 0.86603(0.001) = 0.4999998 - 0.00086603, or about 0.4991337. The difference quotient [0.4991337 - 0.5]/0.001 is about -0.8663, which matches -sin(pi/3), about -0.8660, closely.

The wave picture used for sine extends naturally here too. Cosine reaches its peak of 1 at x = 0, and right at that peak its slope should be momentarily flat, which matches -sin(0) = 0 exactly. As x increases toward pi/2, cosine is sliding downhill toward 0, so its slope should be negative there, and indeed -sin(pi/2) = -1, a fully negative slope at the steepest point of the descent. Watching the sign of -sin x track the rising and falling of the cos x graph this closely, at every point rather than just the ones checked numerically, is a good habit for building intuition alongside the algebraic derivation.

It is also worth noting that unlike the root and rational functions from earlier sections, sin x and cos x are defined for every real number x, with no denominators to worry about and no domain restrictions of any kind. Their derivatives, cos x and -sin x, inherit that same unrestricted domain, since they too are built entirely from sine and cosine with no division involved. That changes as soon as tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant enter the picture, since each of those is a ratio or reciprocal built from sine and cosine, and the quotient rule and reciprocal rule already covered are exactly the tools needed to carry these two building block results forward into the rest of trigonometry, restrictions and all.
